name: Draco
introduction: is the Dragon, often identified with Ladon, who guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides. It is the eighth-largest constellation, a long, winding chain of stars coiling between the Big and Little Dippers, with a head of four stars near Vega. From mid-northern latitudes, Draco never sets.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: Draco has watched the sky turn for thousands of years. Around 2700 BC, the faint star [Thuban](hip:68756) was the pole star, and some passages in the Great Pyramid of Giza seem aligned with it. The north pole of the ecliptic, the center around which Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, also lies in Draco.

In 1728, while studying [Eltanin](hip:87833), which passed directly overhead in London, James Bradley discovered the aberration of light: tiny shifts in star positions caused by Earth’s motion. It was the first direct proof that Earth orbits the Sun.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Eltanin](hip:87833) and [Rastaban](hip:85670) are the dragon’s eyes. Eltanin, an orange giant 154 light-years away, is the brightest star; in about 1.5 million years, it will pass within 28 light-years of the Sun and become one of the brightest stars in the sky.
[Altais](hip:94376) and [Athebyne](hip:80331) mark the dragon’s coils, and [Chi Draconis](hip:89937), 26 light-years away, is a close binary of two Sun-like stars.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: The Cat’s Eye Nebula, NGC 6543, is one of the most intricate planetary nebulae known, with shells and jets of gas around a dying star, close to the ecliptic pole. Draco also contains the Draco Dwarf, a satellite galaxy rich in dark matter, and the Tadpole Galaxy, with a long tail of stars. Each October, the Draconid meteors, debris from Comet Giacobini–Zinner, radiate from the dragon’s head.
